lec05kp20-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp20-u01-p1-title.text: The kernel trick is not only for the SVM: any inner-product algorithm can be kernelized in three steps

lec05kp20-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP19 used the kernel trick on the SVM. Can any other algorithm that uses only inner products be lifted the same way?

lec05kp20-u01-p1-term:核化.name: term:Kernelization
lec05kp20-u01-p1-term:核化.text: **Kernelization**: replacing the inner products of an algorithm by a kernel function, giving a nonlinear version in the original space.

lec05kp20-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p1-c1.text: **The three-step recipe**: (1) rewrite the algorithm with inner products only; (2) replace each inner product by $K$; (3) write the solution as a combination of training points.

lec05kp20-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p1-c2.text: **The weight vector**: it is never computed; $K$ is as in KP19 and must meet the Mercer condition.

lec05kp20-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp20-u01-p2-title.text: The kernelized Euclidean classifier: compare which class mean is closer in the kernel space

lec05kp20-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p2-bridge.text: The first example of the three-step recipe: the nearest-mean rule uses only inner products, so how is it kernelized?

lec05kp20-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p2-c1.text: **The rule**: compare $\|\phi(x)-\mu_1\|^2$ and $\|\phi(x)-\mu_2\|^2$, with $\mu_k$ the mean of $\phi(x_i)$ over class $k$; expanding and cancelling $\|\phi(x)\|^2$ leaves $\langle\phi(x),\mu_2-\mu_1\rangle>\theta$ with $\theta=(\|\mu_2\|^2-\|\mu_1\|^2)/2$; true means class 2.

lec05kp20-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p2-c2.text: **With kernels**: $\tfrac1{N_2}\sum_{y_i=-1}K(x,x_i)-\tfrac1{N_1}\sum_{y_i=+1}K(x,x_i)>\theta$; $2\theta$ is the mean kernel value within class 2 minus that within class 1.

lec05kp20-u01-p2-c3.name: u01-p2-c3
lec05kp20-u01-p2-c3.text: **Recognize it**: the two sums are Parzen estimates (KP18) with a Gaussian kernel.

lec05kp20-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp20-u01-p3-title.text: On the rings: Gaussian kernel 97.4%, linear kernel 48.8%, and only 79.8% with θ dropped

lec05kp20-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p3-bridge.text: The two sums look like Parzen density estimates. Does θ matter? On the rings, how much do the linear, quadratic and Gaussian kernels and the version without θ get right?

lec05kp20-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-kmeanres
lec05kp20-u01-p3-fig1.text: New-point accuracy of the kernelized Euclidean classifier on rings: linear 48.8%, quadratic 93.8%, Gaussian 97.4% and Gaussian with θ dropped 79.8%.

image.alt: New-point accuracy of the kernelized Euclidean classifier on rings: linear 48.8%, quadratic 93.8%, Gaussian 97.4% and Gaussian with θ dropped 79.8%.

lec05kp20-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p3-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): rings of radius 1 and 2 (sd 0.25), 60 training and 500 new points per class; Gaussian $\gamma=0.5$, quadratic $(x^Tz+1)^2$.

lec05kp20-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp20-u01-p3-c3.text: **Dropping $\theta$** (comparing only the two sums, an equal-prior Parzen comparison): 79.8%. The classes differ in mean kernel value within themselves and $\theta$ corrects for it, so '≈ Parzen' cannot ignore it.

lec05kp20-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp20-u01-p4-title.text: The kernel perceptron: a counter αᵢ per training point, and w is never computed

lec05kp20-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p4-bridge.text: The Gaussian kernel got 97.4% on the rings and 79.8% with θ dropped, but that is a mean rule. The perceptron also uses only inner products: how is it kernelized?

lec05kp20-u01-p4-term:核感知器.name: term:Kernel perceptron
lec05kp20-u01-p4-term:核感知器.text: **Kernel perceptron**: a perceptron run in the kernel space that adds 1 to the counter $\alpha_i$ of a misclassified point instead of computing $w$.

lec05kp20-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p4-c1.text: **Update**: on $y_tg(x_t)\le0$, $w\leftarrow w+y_t\phi(x_t)$; from zero this ends as $w=\sum\alpha_iy_i\phi(x_i)$, $w_0=\sum\alpha_iy_i$.

lec05kp20-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p4-c2.text: **Algorithm**: all $\alpha_i=0$; sweep pass after pass, add 1 to $\alpha_i$ when $y_ig(x_i)\le0$, until a pass has no mistake; $g(x)=\sum\alpha_iy_iK(x,x_i)+\sum\alpha_iy_i$.

lec05kp20-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp20-u01-p5-title.text: By hand: 4 points and the quadratic kernel stop after 3 passes with α=(1,1,1,1) and g(x)=2(x₁²−x₂²)

lec05kp20-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p5-bridge.text: The kernel perceptron adds 1 to $\alpha_i$ at each mistake. Work through 4 points with the quadratic kernel by hand: how many passes, and what is $\alpha$?

lec05kp20-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p5-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): points $(1,0)+$, $(-1,0)+$, $(0,1)-$, $(0,-1)-$ with $K=(x^Tz+1)^2$; no straight line separates them.

lec05kp20-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p5-c2.text: **The run**: pass 1: points 1, 3 and 4 are wrong, $\alpha=(1,0,1,1)$; pass 2: point 2 is wrong, $\alpha=(1,1,1,1)$; pass 3 has no mistake, stop.

lec05kp20-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp20-u01-p5-c3.text: **Result**: summing the four kernels gives $g(x)=2(x_1^2-x_2^2)$, which is $+8$ at $(2,0)$ and $-8$ at $(0,2)$.

lec05kp20-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp20-u01-p6-title.text: A linear perceptron never stops in 500 passes, a kernel perceptron stops in 8, or in 428 when the rings touch

lec05kp20-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p6-bridge.text: The hand run of 4 points with the quadratic kernel stopped after 3 passes. On the rings, how many passes do the linear and the kernel perceptron need?

lec05kp20-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-epochs
lec05kp20-u01-p6-fig1.text: Mistakes per pass: the linear perceptron still errs after 500 passes; the kernel perceptron reaches 0 after 8 passes at sd 0.15 and 428 at sd 0.25.

image.alt: Mistakes per pass: the linear perceptron still errs after 500 passes; the kernel perceptron reaches 0 after 8 passes at sd 0.15 and 428 at sd 0.25.

lec05kp20-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p6-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): rings, 60 training and 500 new points per class; Gaussian $\gamma=0.5$; sd 0.15 (separable) and 0.25 (touching at the edges).

lec05kp20-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p6-c2.text: **Results**: the linear perceptron still errs after 500 passes with 50.0% on new points. Kernel perceptron: sd 0.15 stops after 8 passes with 98.2%; sd 0.25 after 428 with 95.6% and 22 points with $\alpha>0$.

lec05kp20-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp20-u01-p6-c3.text: **Meaning**: it stops in finitely many passes when separable, but needs many more when the classes sit close; for sd 0.25 and one random draw, $\gamma=0.1,2,8$ take 191, 571 and 175 passes.

lec05kp20-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp20-u01-p7-title.text: Four common classification losses: hinge, exponential, logistic and 0/1, plotted against z=y·g(x)

lec05kp20-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p7-bridge.text: The kernel perceptron only asks whether it is wrong, and on the rings it just has to stop. How badly wrong a classification is, what measures it?

lec05kp20-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-losses
lec05kp20-u01-p7-fig1.text: The four losses against z=y·g(x): hinge, exponential, logistic and 0/1, with the exponential steepest on the left.

image.alt: The four losses against z=y·g(x): hinge, exponential, logistic and 0/1, with the exponential steepest on the left.

lec05kp20-u01-p7-term:間隔值.name: term:Margin value
lec05kp20-u01-p7-term:間隔值.text: **Margin value** $z=y\,g(x)$: $z>0$ is correct, $z\le0$ is a mistake, and the more negative the worse.

lec05kp20-u01-p7-term:損失函數.name: term:Loss function
lec05kp20-u01-p7-term:損失函數.text: **Loss function**: a penalty for each $z$; it sets the personality of an algorithm.

lec05kp20-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p7-c2.text: **Where used**: hinge is the SVM soft margin; exponential is used by AdaBoost (KP25); logistic is the negative log-likelihood of the logistic probability model; 0/1 is not differentiable.

lec05kp20-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp20-u01-p8-title.text: The exponential loss punishes badly wrong points hardest: about 2.5 times the hinge loss at z=−2

lec05kp20-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p8-bridge.text: How much do the four losses penalize when $z\le0$? Which one is harshest on badly wrong points?

lec05kp20-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p8-c2.text: **Meaning**: the exponential is steepest on the negative side: $7.389/3=2.46$ times the hinge loss for one badly wrong point; this drives AdaBoost and makes it sensitive to outliers (a weakness on high-Bayes-error tasks per the source, KP25).

lec05kp20-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp20-u01-p8-c3.text: **To remember**: the general recipe is (1) inner products only, (2) replace them by $K$, (3) express the solution as a combination of training points; the weight vector is never computed.

lec05kp20-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp20-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: the logistic loss is only 0.693 at z=0 and must be divided by ln 2 to bound the 0/1 loss

lec05kp20-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p9-bridge.text: The exponential loss is steepest on the negative side. At $z=0$ the logistic loss is 0.693 and the 0/1 loss is 1, so does the logistic loss bound the 0/1 loss?

lec05kp20-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-logup
lec05kp20-u01-p9-fig1.text: The 0/1 loss, the logistic loss and the logistic loss divided by ln 2; at z=0 the logistic is only 0.693 and reaches 1 after dividing by ln 2.

image.alt: The 0/1 loss, the logistic loss and the logistic loss divided by ln 2; at z=0 the logistic is only 0.693 and reaches 1 after dividing by ln 2.

lec05kp20-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp20-u01-p9-c1.text: **Upper bound**: hinge and exponential are never below 0/1; the logistic $\ln(1+e^{-z})$ is only $\ln2=0.693<1$ at $z=0$, so it is not an upper bound.

lec05kp20-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp20-u01-p9-c2.text: **Normalizing**: dividing by $\ln2$ makes it exactly 1 at $z=0$ and at least 1 for $z\le0$, a convex upper bound of 0/1 (the source's normalized logistic).

lec05kp20-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp20-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, the g(x) of the kernel perceptron and its simplification

lec05kp20-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p10-bridge.text: The logistic loss must be divided by $\ln2$ to stay above the upper bound of 0/1. Back to the kernel perceptron to test the $g$ we derived: the hand trace stopped at $\alpha=(1,1,1,1)$, so which class does $x=(1,2)$ get?

lec05kp20-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp20-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 1**: compute $g(x)$ at $x=(1,2)$ from the four kernels; which class?

lec05kp20-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp20-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: simplify $g$ to a formula in $x_1,x_2$ and check Question 1.

lec05kp20-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp20-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2, both ways give −6

lec05kp20-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked to compute $g(x)$ at $x=(1,2)$ from the four kernels and to simplify it. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp20-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp20-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2**: adding the four squares, $g=2(x_1^2+1)-2(x_2^2+1)=2(x_1^2-x_2^2)$; at $x=(1,2)$: $2(1-4)=-6$, the same as Question 1.

lec05kp20-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp20-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: $g>0$ means $|x_1|>|x_2|$, the positive class; the boundary is two diagonal lines, and the four points no line could split are separated.

steps.label: Kernel trick beyond SVM
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The three-step recipe of kernelization, the kernelized Euclidean classifier and its relation to the Parzen estimate, the update and discriminant of the kernel perceptron, the four loss functions and their uses and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number (48.8%, 93.8% and 97.4% for the kernelized Euclidean classifier on rings, 79.8% with theta dropped, the 4-point hand run of 3 passes, the passes and accuracies of the perceptrons, the loss table, logistic divided by ln 2, the practice answer minus 6) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added); the pages state honestly that theta cannot be ignored, that many passes are needed when the classes touch and that the logistic loss needs normalizing to bound the 0/1 loss. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: The three-step recipe
steps.speakerNotes: KP19 used the kernel trick on the SVM. This page asks whether any other algorithm that uses only inner products can be lifted the same way. First kernelization: replacing the inner products of an algorithm by a kernel function, giving a nonlinear version in the original space. The three-step recipe: first rewrite the algorithm with inner products only; second replace each inner product by K; third write the solution as a combination of training points. The weight vector is never computed, and K is as in KP19 and must meet the Mercer condition. The figure shows the recipe. The next page takes the first example: how does the nearest-mean rule, which uses only inner products, get kernelized?

steps.label: The Euclidean rule
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page was the three-step recipe. This page asks how the nearest-mean rule, which uses only inner products, is kernelized. The rule: compare the squared distances from phi of x to the two class means, mu_k being the mean of phi of x_i over class k; expanding and cancelling the squared length of phi of x leaves the inner product of phi of x with mu_2 minus mu_1 above theta. With kernels: the mean kernel value to class 2 minus the mean to class 1 exceeds theta, and 2 theta is the mean kernel value within class 2 minus that within class 1. Recognize it: the two sums look like the Parzen density estimates of KP18, and are exactly that with the Gaussian kernel. The next page asks whether theta matters.

steps.label: Comparison on the rings
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the two sums look like Parzen density estimates. This page asks whether theta matters and how much the linear, quadratic and Gaussian kernels and the version without theta get right on the rings. The setup was designed here: rings of radius 1 and 2 with standard deviation 0.25, 60 training and 500 new points per class; Gaussian gamma 0.5 and the quadratic kernel x transpose z plus 1, squared. Results on new points: linear 48.8%; quadratic 93.8%; Gaussian 97.4%. Dropping theta and comparing only the two sums, an equal-prior Parzen comparison, gives 79.8%. The classes differ in mean kernel value within themselves and theta corrects for it, so the source's approximately Parzen cannot ignore theta. The next page turns to the perceptron.

steps.label: The kernel perceptron
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the kernelized Euclidean classifier is only a mean rule. This page asks how the update of the perceptron, which also uses only inner products, looks after kernelization. First the kernel perceptron: a perceptron run in the kernel space that adds 1 to the counter alpha_i of a misclassified point instead of computing w. The update: when y_t times g of x_t is at most 0, w becomes w plus y_t times phi of x_t; starting from zero, w ends as the sum of alpha_i y_i phi of x_i and w0 as the sum of alpha_i y_i. The algorithm: all alphas zero, sweep the training points pass after pass, add 1 on a mistake, until a whole pass has no mistake. Why it matters: a linear perceptron converges only if the classes are linearly separable, and after a kernel map to high dimension Cover's theorem of KP14 makes separability likely. The next page works through 4 points by hand.

steps.label: A hand trace
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the kernel perceptron adds 1 to alpha_i at each mistake. This page asks, by working through 4 points with the quadratic kernel by hand, how many passes it takes and what alpha is. The setup was designed here: points (1, 0) and (-1, 0) are positive, (0, 1) and (0, -1) are negative, and K is x transpose z plus 1, squared; no straight line separates them. The run: in pass 1 points 1, 3 and 4 are wrong and alpha is (1, 0, 1, 1); in pass 2 point 2 is wrong and alpha is (1, 1, 1, 1); pass 3 has no mistake, so stop. The result: summing the four kernels gives g equal to 2 times x1 squared minus x2 squared, which is 8 at (2, 0) and minus 8 at (0, 2). The next page asks how many passes the rings need.

steps.label: The rings experiment
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the hand run of 4 points with the quadratic kernel stopped after 3 passes. This page asks how many passes the linear and the kernel perceptron need on the rings. The setup was designed here: rings, 60 training and 500 new points per class; Gaussian gamma 0.5; standard deviation 0.15, separable, and 0.25, touching at the edges. Results: the linear perceptron still errs after 500 passes with 50.0% on new points. The kernel perceptron with standard deviation 0.15 stops after 8 passes with 98.2% on new points; with 0.25 it stops after 428 passes with 95.6% and 22 points with alpha above 0. The meaning is that it stops in finitely many passes when separable but needs many more when the classes sit close; gamma of 0.1, 2 and 8 take 191, 571 and 175 passes. The next page asks how an algorithm measures how wrong a classification is.

steps.label: Loss functions
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the kernel perceptron only asks whether it is wrong, and on the rings it just has to stop. This page asks what measures how badly wrong a classification is. First the margin value z equal to y times g of x: z above 0 is correct, at most 0 is a mistake, and the more negative the worse. The loss function gives each z a penalty and sets the personality of an algorithm. The four: hinge, the larger of 1 minus z and 0; exponential, e to the minus z; logistic, the log of 1 plus e to the minus z; and 0/1, which is 1 when z is at most 0. Where used: hinge is the SVM soft margin; exponential is used by AdaBoost in KP25; logistic is the negative log-likelihood of the logistic probability model; 0/1 is not differentiable. The figure shows the four curves. The next page asks how much they differ when a point is badly wrong.

steps.label: The personality of a loss
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the four losses against z. This page asks how much they penalize when z is at most 0 and which is harshest on badly wrong points. Values: at z equal to minus 2, hinge 3, exponential 7.389, logistic 2.127 and 0/1 equal to 1; at z equal to 0, 1, 1, 0.693 and 1; at z equal to 2, 0, 0.135, 0.127 and 0. The meaning: the exponential is steepest on the negative side and one badly wrong point costs 7.389 over 3, which is 2.46 times the hinge loss; this drives AdaBoost and is also its weakness on high-Bayes-error tasks, as the source says, to be seen in KP25. To remember: the general recipe has three steps, inner products only, replace them by K, and express the solution as a combination of training points; the weight vector is never computed. The next extension page asks why the logistic loss is divided by ln 2.

steps.label: Extension: logistic bound
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the exponential loss is steepest on the negative side. This extension asks whether the logistic loss bounds the 0/1 loss, given that at z equal to 0 it is 0.693 while the 0/1 loss is 1. Upper bound: hinge and exponential are never below 0/1; the logistic is only ln 2, which is 0.693 and below 1, at z equal to 0, so it is not an upper bound. Normalizing: dividing by ln 2 makes it exactly 1 at z equal to 0 and at least 1 for z at most 0, a convex upper bound of 0/1, the source's normalized logistic. Check: at z equal to minus 2, 2.127 over 0.693 is 3.069; at z equal to minus 1, 1.313 over 0.693 is 1.895, both above 1. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the logistic loss must be divided by ln 2 to stay above the upper bound of 0/1. This page poses a new question: the hand trace stopped at alpha equal to (1, 1, 1, 1), so which class does x equal to (1, 2) get? The setup: points (1, 0) and (-1, 0) are positive, (0, 1) and (0, -1) are negative, K is x transpose z plus 1, squared, and all alphas are 1. Question 1: compute g at x equal to (1, 2) from the four kernels; which class? Question 2: simplify g to a formula in x1 and x2 and check Question 1. Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: K of x with (1, 0) is 4, with (-1, 0) is 0, with (0, 1) is 9 and with (0, -1) is 1; the sum of alpha y is 0; g is 4 plus 0 minus 9 minus 1 plus 0, which is minus 6, the negative class. Question 2: adding the four squares, g is 2 times x1 squared plus 1, minus 2 times x2 squared plus 1, which is 2 times x1 squared minus x2 squared; at x equal to (1, 2) it is 2 times 1 minus 4, which is minus 6, the same as Question 1. Check: g above 0 means the absolute value of x1 exceeds that of x2, the positive class; the boundary is two diagonal lines, and the four points no line could split are separated. That finishes going beyond the SVM; the next knowledge point looks at the representer theorem and sparsification.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP20: beyond the SVM, the general kernel trick and the kernel perceptron (undergraduate, self-study)
